(52) "In a pressing situation," etc. It is not considered a pressing situation unless there are no 4 valid species anywhere in the city. But if one's fellow has valid species, even though he himself cannot otherwise obtain them, this is not considered a pressing situation. He must make the effort to recite the blessing over his fellow's set if it is lent to him, and if he cannot perform the naanuim with his fellow's set, he should perform the naanuim with his own. [Later authorities]

(53) "All invalid species," etc. Meaning species invalid because of a defect. But items invalid because they are not of the required species, such as hadas shoteh or tzafzefah, or a grafted species, are invalid even in a pressing situation, because people may come to err and use them regularly. The same applies to stolen species; they are invalid even in a pressing situation. If there are no valid 4 species anywhere in the city, he should take whatever 2 or 3 species are available and perform all the naanuim, and the shaliach tzibbur should do likewise, but without a blessing. One may not take a different species in place of a missing one, lest people err in future years. With only 3 of the proper species, however, there is no such concern, because everyone knows that 4 species are required.

(54) "They are taken and no blessing is recited." They are taken even on the first day, so that the mitzvah of lulav not be forgotten from Israel. No blessing is recited because the act is only commemorative.

(55) "A dry lulav." Rambam's view is that even in a pressing situation leniency applies only to a dry lulav, but not to the other species when they are dry, as explained below. He also holds that one should be lenient only regarding dryness, not regarding other invalidating defects, even in a pressing situation.

(56) "Even when others have moist ones." The reason is that this concerns countries where fully fresh lulavim are not available, and the dry lulavim are not completely dry either, meaning they have not reached the point where they crumble under the fingernail. The same applies to hadasim that have not reached the stage where their appearance turns white. Thus the "fresh" and "dry" examples are nearly alike, and therefore the custom is to recite the blessing over one's own.

(57) "Even a dry hadas." Because fully fresh hadasim are likewise not readily available. Aravot, however, are commonly available fresh. Regarding an etrog, according to this opinion they did not wish to be lenient, because Scripture explicitly calls it "the fruit of a beautiful tree."

(58) "And one may rely upon them in a pressing situation." The later authorities agree in practice that in a pressing situation we may rely upon those authorities who hold that one may recite a blessing over all 4 species when they are dry. There are 4 distinctions. If no fresh species are available in the city and only dry ones are available, all 4 species are taken with a blessing. If he has completely dry species while others have completely fresh species, the blessing is recited only over the fresh ones, and even after the fact he did not fulfill the obligation by blessing over the fully dry ones. In countries where fully fresh lulavim and hadasim are unavailable, and the dry ones are not completely dry as explained above, one may recite the blessing over the dry ones he has even initially. Where others possess fully fresh species, however, initially he should not recite the blessing over his own dry species even if they are not fully dry. If he already did so, he should take the fresh species belonging to others again without another blessing.

(59) "He may take," etc. See Magen Avraham, who asks what Rama adds to the Mechaber's ruling above in seif 6. Bikurei Yaakov explains that the Mechaber wrote that in a pressing situation, where no valid set is currently available, one should take the invalid set without a blessing. We still would not know the law if a valid set will become available later, but at present is not in his possession, for example where another person is presently reciting Hallel with his valid lulav and has promised to lend it to him afterward. Could he meanwhile take his own invalid lulav during Hallel, or might that create a doubtful blessing later when he takes the valid set? Rama therefore teaches that he may initially take the invalid set without a blessing, because it is certainly invalid, and afterward he may recite the blessing over the valid set when it becomes available.

"And some say that one who," etc. Maharshal writes that on the seventh day, even one who has no lulav should circle with the aravah. However, this appears as religious ostentation. Nevertheless, if there is no lulav anywhere in the city, they should circle with the aravah. [Bach]

"On the seventh day," etc. As explained afterward, because on the festival judgment concerns water. See Taz, seif katan 1, and so too Tur. As stated in the first chapter of Rosh Hashanah, "Pour water before Me," etc., and we rule like the first Tanna that the water libation is performed only for 7 days. Therefore the seventh day is treated in some respects like Yom Kippur, and in some respects like Yom Tov, as stated in the Mishnah, chapter 4 of Sukkah, where they greatly increased the rejoicing, including the children's lulavim. All the days of judgment are also Yom Tov, namely the 4 periods of judgment during the year. So too in the Midrash and Yerushalmi, first chapter of Rosh Hashanah: "What nation is like this nation, which knows the nature of its God," etc.

"And Nishmat is not recited." See Rashbam, Perek Arvei Pesachim, 102b, end of the page, s.v. "And Shmuel said," and the continuation there.

"And they recite Mizmor LeTodah." As stated in the second chapter of Beitzah, 19b.

"And they say," etc. As explained above.

"They wrote," etc. For then the person's judgment is completed together with the judgment concerning water, because water gives life. The Sages said that 10 things are called "living," etc., and Scripture states, "The shadows flee," and, "Their shade has departed from them."

"In the moonlight." Because the moon is appointed over the waters, and the waters increase and diminish with its waning and waxing.

"And some hold," etc. As stated in the last chapter of Horayot and the first chapter of Keritot.

"And more," etc. As stated in Perek Arvei Pesachim; see there.

"And some have the custom," etc. See Magen Avraham concerning the custom in our country, and as stated in the Yerushalmi cited above, that they wear white garments.

"And they increase supplications," etc. As explained above.

1) [Seif 1] "If one is uncertain whether he recited Kriat Shema, he repeats it and recites the blessings," etc. This is because we rule that Kriat Shema is Torah-level, and regarding any Torah-level doubt one recites the blessing. Beit Yosef in the name of Rabbeinu Yonah; Levush; Bach; Perishah; Taz, seif katan 1.

Although above, siman 17, seif 2, we stated that a tumtum and androgynous are obligated in tzitzit because of doubt and should wrap themselves without a blessing, even though tzitzit is Torah-level, Derishah explains that the cases are entirely different. There the doubt is whether the person is subject to the obligation at all, and therefore no blessing is recited because perhaps the person is halachically a woman. Here, however, he is certainly obligated by Torah law to recite Kriat Shema. Since he does not know clearly whether he already recited it, he repeats it and recites the blessings. Knesset HaGedolah writes likewise in Hagahot Beit Yosef.

Nevertheless, there remains room to ask: this does not resemble an ordinary birkat hamitzvah, where one blesses over the performance of the mitzvah. Here one does not recite a blessing formulated "to recite Kriat Shema," as explained above in siman 66, letter 27. Why, then, should the blessings be repeated because of the doubtful mitzvah?

Responsa Rashba, siman 320, gives another explanation. He writes: It is still difficult regarding Rambam, who explicitly holds that all blessings are rabbinic. Whenever one is uncertain whether he performed the mitzvah, even where the mitzvah itself is Torah-level, or where he is uncertain whether he is obligated at all, such as a child born without a visible foreskin or the eighth day of Sukkot, which is doubtful whether it is the seventh, no blessing is recited. Rambam wrote similarly to the sages of Lunel. Rashba suggests that according to Rambam the original enactment of Kriat Shema was that whenever one is obligated to recite it, he should recite it initially together with its blessings, unless a special circumstance alters the normal order, such as the Temple reading, where only 1 blessing was said. Alternatively, because Kriat Shema is also Torah study, as with Rabbi, who would pass his hands over his eyes and accept the yoke of Heaven through the first verse. Ordinarily, however, when one recites Kriat Shema, he should recite it together with its blessings, just as one who reads after its proper time "has not lost," which the Gemara explains to mean that he has not lost the blessings.

Rashba further suggests that Rambam derived this from R' Elazar's statement: if one is uncertain whether he recited Kriat Shema, he repeats and recites it. Since the Gemara simply says "he repeats and recites," this implies that he recites all the paragraphs, even though according to some only the first verse is Torah-level. It did not say that he should repeat only the first verse while omitting the rabbinic remainder. The reason is that once one is obligated to recite Kriat Shema, he recites it according to the basic form of the rabbinic enactment. Rashba adds that he believes he heard this reasoning from his pious teacher regarding why one repeats all the paragraphs and does not suffice with the first verse alone, and perhaps Rambam extended the same principle to the blessings. Kesef Mishneh, chapter 2 of Hilchot Kriat Shema, law 13; Knesset HaGedolah; Olat Tamid, letter 2; Magen Avraham, seif katan 1; Eliyah Rabbah, letter 1. Pri Chadash, however, agrees with the explanation of Knesset HaGedolah. See also Yad Aharon and Maamar Mordechai, letter 2; for practical differences between the explanations, see Pri Megadim, Eshel Avraham, letter 1.

If he knows that he recited the first verse but is uncertain whether he recited the remainder, Magen Avraham writes that Lechem Chamudot, siman 40, appears to hold that he need not repeat it. Yet siman 64, seif 3, implies that he must repeat it. Magen Avraham therefore concludes that the enactment from the outset was that he should repeat. Eliyah Rabbah and Shulchan Aruch HaRav cite this. Shulchan Aruch HaRav writes that the same applies where he knows he recited the first paragraph but is uncertain regarding the second; he must repeat the second. Maamar Mordechai writes that even Lechem Chamudot means only that the blessings need not be repeated; the paragraphs themselves should be repeated without blessings.

If he is certain that he recited the first 2 paragraphs but is uncertain whether he recited Parashat Tzitzit and Emet VeYatziv, Bach writes that he must repeat Parashat Tzitzit and the blessing Emet VeYatziv. If, however, he is certain that he recited all 3 paragraphs and is uncertain only regarding the preceding blessings and Emet VeYatziv, he need not repeat the blessings. Taz, seif katan 1; Magen Avraham; Eliyah Rabbah, letter 2, who rejects Olat Tamid's view that one should recite Parashat Tzitzit without Emet VeYatziv. Shulchan Aruch HaRav likewise agrees. Shaagat Aryeh, siman 11, however, rules like Olat Tamid that only Parashat Tzitzit should be repeated, without the blessing Emet VeYatziv. Although Erech HaShulchan, letter 2, disagrees with Shaagat Aryeh, the matter remains doubtful. Therefore in practice it appears that he should recite Parashat Tzitzit and Emet VeYatziv, but should not conclude the blessing with the Divine Name. Rather, he should say "Baruch Ga'al Yisrael," because of the rule that in cases of doubt regarding blessings we are lenient. The same applies at night if he is uncertain whether he recited Parashat Tzitzit and Emet VeEmunah: he should recite them, but should not conclude with the Divine Name. See Shulchan Aruch HaRav and Shaagat Aryeh there.

If he is uncertain whether he recited Kriat Shema but knows that he recited Emet VeYatziv, Tosafot write that he does not repeat Kriat Shema. Even if he knows that he merely contemplated Emet VeYatziv, Responsa Beit Yaakov, siman 135, and Eliyah Rabbah, letter 2, rule that he does not repeat. Maamar Mordechai, however, discusses this at length, cites the responsum of Beit Yaakov, disagrees, and writes that only if he knows he actually recited Emet VeYatziv need he not repeat. If he knows merely that he thought it, he must recite Kriat Shema with its blessings. Even where he knows that he recited Emet VeYatziv but is uncertain about Kriat Shema, Maamar Mordechai writes that it is proper to repeat Kriat Shema without the blessings. See also Pri Megadim, Eshel Avraham, letter 1.

Regarding the Torah-level obligation of Kriat Shema, there are several opinions. Some hold that only the first verse is Torah-level; this appears to be Maran's view in Beit Yosef at the end of siman 63. Others hold that the entire first paragraph is Torah-level. Others hold that the first 2 paragraphs are Torah-level as Kriat Shema, while Parashat Tzitzit is Torah-level because of the obligation to remember the Exodus from Egypt. Pri Chadash discusses this at length and inclines to hold that the first 2 paragraphs are Torah-level, bringing proofs. Shaagat Aryeh, siman 2, disagrees and writes that only the first paragraph is Torah-level. Knesset HaGedolah in Hagahot HaTur cites an opinion that all the paragraphs of Kriat Shema are Torah-level. See also Magen Avraham, siman 63, seif katan 8.

Although the Sages enacted that one must recite all 3 paragraphs even according to the view that they are not all Torah-level, there is a practical difference for one under great pressure who fears that the proper time for Kriat Shema will pass. As written above in siman 67, letter 52, he should recite Kriat Shema without the blessings, and afterward, when he has time, recite it again with its blessings and pray. If he has sufficient time, he should recite all 3 paragraphs in order to fulfill Kriat Shema in its proper time according to all opinions. If he is pressed, he should recite the first 2 paragraphs. If he is extremely pressed, he should recite at least the first paragraph to the extent he is able. See also what was written at the end of siman 46.

"That they do not." See Taz. The Mechaber omitted the phrase "all day," etc. Taz concludes that where women have the custom to refrain from melacha throughout the entire day, this may perhaps apply for the entire day. Maharil implies that even men refrain while the Chanukah lights are burning. On the first and last day, in places where the custom is to prohibit melacha throughout the entire day even for men, they should not be permitted to work. See Eliyah Rabbah, letter 11, and Magen Avraham, seif katan 2.

There is also a reason to refrain while the lights are burning, as a visible reminder that one may not derive benefit from their light. See Tur.

(5) "Therefore one must put in," etc. This implies that if he kindled some time after sunset, he need not put in enough oil for the full standard measure, but only enough to burn until pedestrian traffic has ceased from the marketplace. All this follows the Talmudic situation, where the publicizing of the miracle was directed toward passersby. Nowadays, when the recognition is primarily for the members of the household, he always requires the standard measure. [Pri Chadash] Even if he lights after pedestrian traffic has already ceased, he still needs this standard measure. [Pri Megadim]

(6) "The measure." Even nowadays one requires this measure. If he puts in much more oil so that the lamp burns longer, there is no additional mitzvah in doing so. With wax candles, however, there is an enhancement of the mitzvah when the candles are long, although they should not be excessively large. Beit Yosef writes in the name of Orchot Chaim that if on the second night a person recited the blessing and lit only 1 lamp, he should afterward light another lamp without another blessing. Pri Megadim inclines that even if he initially intended to light only 1 and afterward another lamp became available, he should still not recite an additional blessing, because by strict law only 1 lamp is obligatory and the others are merely an enhancement.

(7) "He may extinguish it," etc. He designates the oil for the mitzvah only for the amount required to burn for half an hour. Therefore afterward he may extinguish it and benefit from the remaining oil. Nevertheless, several later authorities agree that initially it is proper to stipulate that he designates only the amount needed for the required burning time, because some authorities hold that if he poured in the oil without stipulation, he designated all of it for the mitzvah.

(8) "To use its light," etc. Some are stringent that while the lamps are burning one may never use their light, even after the required time, because an observer may not know the distinction between the required burning time and afterward.

(9) "Since nowadays we light indoors." Meaning that the recognition is therefore only for the household members.

(10) "He need not." Rather, he should light when the members of the household are gathered together. Once the time for lighting has arrived, even Torah study is forbidden, all the more so eating and drinking and other activities; even if he began earlier, he must stop.

(11) "All night." Until dawn, with a blessing. This applies specifically when members of the household are awake. If they are sleeping, he should not recite a blessing for them, but should light without a blessing, because just as in the Talmudic period one recited the blessing only while publicizing the miracle to others, so too for us. If he returns home before dawn and finds the household asleep, it is proper to wake them so that he can light with a blessing.

(12) "Like all other people." Meaning that on the second night he lights 2 lamps and on the third night 3. We do not say that because this person's second night is effectively his first, he should light only 1. [Darkei Moshe]

"Freed." According to Beit Yosef, even slaves who have not been freed, but who underwent brit milah and immersion for the sake of slavery, are obligated in reading the Megillah. Rabbeinu Shimshon disagrees. Re'em, in his novellae to Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, likewise writes that according to Sefer Mitzvot Gadol slaves are not obligated in reading the Megillah.

Therefore it appears to me, without hesitation, that according to all opinions slaves who have not been freed are not obligated in reading the Megillah. My teacher wrote that even slaves who have not been freed are obligated, but they cannot discharge others. Nevertheless, the primary view appears to me to be that they are not obligated in its reading at all, as stated above.
